Ed Soph

Ed Soph has balanced a successful career in jazz as a valued drummer and distinguished educator. He has shared the bandstand with Woody Herman, Joe Williams, Clark Terry, and numerous other jazz luminaries.
Ed was interviewed via Zoom on February 9, 2024 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and a real pleasure to have Ed Soph with me today, drummer and jazz educator, and one of the early students of jazz education. Am I correct? North Texas State way back?
Right. Actually when I was there, I was there from 1963 through ’68 and there was no jazz degree yet.
Yeah, you read my mind. Because I was at SUNY Fredonia, graduated in ’72, and there was, although we had a band, there was no jazz education either.
Right, yeah.
And I read that you switched to a different major. What was the reason for that?

Yeah I switched, became an English major in my junior year. Let me — how to put this — I knew I wanted to play music but I realized that the degrees as set up at North Texas at that time really had nothing to do with what I wanted to do musically other than getting me the great opportunity of working under Mr. Breeden in the One O’clock Lab Band, and having some wonderful classmates to work with as well. But my thinking was this is probably the only time I’m ever going to be in an institution of higher learning, at least as a student. So I chose to get as broad an education as I could. Because back then if you went to North Texas it was to either become — well it was primarily to become an educator. A band leader. High school band leader, that sort of thing. And in fact I had originally gone there in hopes of studying timpani because timpani was my great love and I had visions of playing in a great orchestra. But when I got to North Texas I auditioned for the orchestra and they said, “Okay Mr. Soph, you’ll play timpani.” And so that first rehearsal I played timpani. Came into the second rehearsal and, “Mr. Soph, today you’ll play wood block.” And I thought uh oh, this is not how you get into the New York Philharmonic.
Now don’t you think there’s something ironic about that because wasn’t your first quote drumset a woodblock and a —

Yeah, yeah, very true. I didn’t think of that. So at any rate I decided that if I really wanted to become a timpanist I would have tried to get into Juilliard or Curtis or Manhattan, obviously a conservatory. So I wanted to get as broad an education as I could so I

changed my major. And I had some incredibly stimulating classes with some really wonderful professors. This was the days before classes consisted of 300 students and one was just a number and fill in the blanks and bubble tests were not used.
Bubble tests. Yes.
Yeah, and the teachers expected you to engage them.
Your parents were supportive of both those decisions? First a music path and then your changing of majors?
Oh yeah, yeah. My parents were always supportive. My mother was always a bit worried as mothers can be, but my father was always a thousand percent behind me.
And I understand he was a musician as well, or at least a jazz fan?

Yeah, well he was an incredible jazz fan and record collector. And he belonged to a record club in Tulsa, a bunch of record collectors. And to relax he played ragtime. He had all the Scott Joplin and music sheets. And that’s how I started playing. My first gig was accompanying my father on that wood block.
Now tell me about, there’s this rumor going around that you borrowed someone’s hubcap to make a cymbal. Is that true?

Yeah that’s true. Yeah. It was a neighbor about two doors down who had one of those big black ominous Packards. And I decided I needed and wanted a cymbal. So I took a hubcap, and then got a ball peen hammer and beat the hell out of it. I had a cymbal. So I caught hell for that.
How old were you then?
I was probably six.
Oh six. I was wondering when you started — this is an assumption on my part — that you started fantasizing about this wonderful drumset, that if only I could have one.

Oh that was when I was in junior high school probably and got my first Gretsch catalogue. But I think the real genesis of the attraction was at Mrs. Rumbal’s nursery school in Tulsa, Oklahoma. And we had a marching band. And I was assigned what they called back then rhythm sticks. They were red of course, and were serrated so you could also make sounds by rubbing them like that. And she also had me play cymbals. And I still have one of the cymbals, it’s a little tiny cymbal about that big with a big wooden knob so your little hand and hold on to it. And I just couldn’t wait ‘til we marched every day. We’d march around the school and I’d either be playing my cymbals or my rhythm sticks. And I think that’s where I first really got that sensation of playing rhythm and doing it with other people. So that’s really where it all started, and everything else just sort of came into place, my father playing ragtime piano, there being music constantly in the house. When we sat down to dinner he’d put a record on and we’d listen to it and talk about it. My mother as well. He would take me to — there were some great traditional

jazz players in Tulsa at the time. And he would take me to some of their gigs and I’d listen to that and then on a number of occasions we’d go to an African-American church and listen to the music there. And we all know the kind of joyous sounds that come out of that. So that really, really enticed me as well.

When you went to the African-American church, did you get an impression that — not exactly sure how to phrase this, but it might have something to do with your years of teaching — that some people are born with an inherent sense — I’m not going to say a sense of rhythm, I’m going to say an ability to hear it and then react to it. And some people aren’t.

Well to one degree or another I think that if a person can march in time then — or speak in time, recite something in time — that then in some form or another they can express that gift physically. But where the breakdown comes, I know so many people, aspiring drummers, who have such an incredible passion for the instrument and for the music, but that passion and desire is not matched by physical ability. And when I was at North Texas I had 32 students per semester. And invariably over the years there were — at the top there was maybe two or three students who were naturals, who had the coordination that came naturally. And then there was a wide breadth of students in the middle that could either, depending upon the success of the teacher, could either continue to expand or remain where they were. And then at the bottom, and I shouldn’t say bottom, I mean this is more — let’s think of it that way — there were the people who would have given whatever they needed to give to play well. But for some reason just physically could not get it together. Either inability to hold sticks in a way that allowed the body to move freely — I mean there’s so many variables involved that to make a blanket statement that some people have it and some people don’t, I don’t know if I would agree with that. I think there’s levels, like there are with every other ability. Some people have great memories, some people have mediocre memories. Some people can recite poetry well, some people can’t. You know. So I think everybody has a potential. There’s so many elements that go into it. Exposure obviously at an early age, and then early teaching experiences, whether or not early teachers encourage the student to discover for him- or herself rather than the teacher being dictatorial and saying this is the right way, all the others are wrong. And I mean this just doesn’t go for improvised music, it goes for any kind of music. It’s the imagination that makes the musician.

You must be reading my notes here because I had a question about that and what methods you might have used to lay the groundwork to increase the chances that a student could be successful in improvising and have a creative spirit?
Okay, well for me the defining factor is how well one listens and perceives sound. And there is a very corny adage which is very true is if you can’t say it you can’t play it. So

my teaching over the years became less and less visual, meaning exercises out of a book, and more and more aural. And what I found was that another impediment to one’s learning ability was the ability to internalize the music and especially as a jazz player. Because you know when a drummer is playing the tune and when the drummer is just playing his licks. When you listen to somebody like Roy Haynes and hear how he orchestrates the tune, I mean it’s right there. Billy Higgins, Philly Joe, all the great drummers up to Brian Blade today and on. They’re playing the music. They’re not playing the drums. So my thrust with the student now is to get them to be able to vocalize, say just as an example, a Charlie Parker tune. Something simple like “Billie’s Bounce.” And when they first sing it they go [scats] right? So they baby talk it. So I say okay find a recording of it, listen to Mr. Parker and the other horns, and get to the point where you can vocalize a reasonable facsimile of the horn. Because as a drummer you have to be an inner horn player. Because those are the people whom you accompany. And just like I tell horn players. You need to learn something about drums and how to listen to drums, because those are the people you’re playing with. So at any rate, yeah, so I get them to vocalize. And if they can internalize that, some people can, some people cannot. Some people do it easily, some people give up very quickly. And it’s like learning a language obviously. And once they’ve got that I say okay, let’s go to the drums. Now you be Charlie Parker only instead of playing an alto saxophone you’re playing a snare drum. Let me hear you play the snare drum with the same flow as Mr. Parker gets with air. I want to hear you get it with motion. See if you can translate [scats] not into [scats] but [scats] right? And they struggle, just as anybody does with something new, but that’s where it all comes from is the struggle. You say, “Okay — it doesn’t sound like Bird, does it. “No man, it doesn’t at all.” I say, “Are you uptight? Are you tense?” “Oh yeah. I’m trying as hard as I can.” Well quit trying. Quit trying. Just let the sticks dance on the drums and then you might make some remarks like, “Hey, look at your hand. Look how tightly it’s holding the stick. Just hold the stick so that, like if you were picking up something that was very fragile. Don’t squeeze it, just let it rest in your hand. Same way if you were an artist you would use a paint brush.” Boom, all these different avenues of connections that you try to make. And lo and behold there it comes. And once you’ve got the melody and you can play it on the snare, then you say okay, let’s add some accompaniment to it. Let’s put a ride cymbal here, and let’s put a hi-hat on two and four, and let’s outline the melody between the snare drum and the bass drum. And all of a sudden they go, “Wow man, I sound like Philly Joe.” And you say, “Well almost.” But the point is using music as the model — using an auditory model not a visual one.
Yeah I was going to ask right at the beginning of this wonderful description you said, “aural.” I’m assuming you’re going A-U-R-A-L. Correct?
Yeah. Ears.
Yeah. Because if there’s a lot like oral history and so forth.

Oh yeah. That’s important too, that that’s the other thing. I don’t make any value judgments because invariably they’re wrong in some form or another. But what I will say is that the hardest thing to do with most students is to get them to listen to the past. Because there’s such great peer pressure to be hip and current. And I talk to my students, I say, “When I was a kid and my father would bring home at first 78s but later on 33-1/3 LPs” and I said, “I would play those damn things until I, without knowing, I was singing horn solos. You know? I quit listening to the drums, quit listening to my instrument, and started listening to the band.” And I said, “That was so valuable.” And I said, “Even more so, my first drum hero was Baby Dodds.” And they go, “Who’s Baby Dod —” No they don’t do that, so I say, “Do you know Baby Dodds?” “Oh yeah, yeah, he’s considered the father of jazz drumming.” And then of course that’s my chance. I say, “Okay, play me time the way Baby Dodds did.” Uh oh. I say, “That’s your mistake. You know names but you don’t know the music that goes with the name.”
And that is increasingly, in my experience — where now it’s, “Yes, I’ve seen it on YouTube.” And considering most people’s attention span maybe they watched Baby Dodds for 30 seconds.

That’s what I was getting at when I got a little off track there about listening to a recording. We’d listen — we didn’t have YouTube. And this is not saying oh let’s go back to the good old days, it’s just a matter of we had no choice but to listen to that record over and over and over and over and realizing that every time we listened to it we heard something new. It’s like reading Huckleberry Finn when you’re 12 years old and then reading Huckleberry Finn when you’re 50 years old. A whole different ballgame. Well it’s the same way with this music, whether it’s jazz or classical or anything. Because it’s not just obviously the hands and feet that develop, it’s the ears, which is the bottom line for all of us. So I’ve got to say you don’t need to practice your drums, you need to practice your ears too. And you go back and listen to Baby Dodds and you’ll hear Baby Dodds playing some of the same rhythms that Jack DeJohnette plays or Elvin Jones played. You’ll start to hook into the tradition. It’s all there it’s just voiced differently and moved around in different ways on the kit, but that basic groove is right back there with Baby Dodds. So getting them to go to the past is difficult because their peers are all saying, “Hey man, you’ve got to listen to this latest —” so-and-so. And then the other thing is just lighting, if it’s not already lit try to light their flame of curiosity. And where this came in, a kid came in for his lesson one day and I said, “Hey do you get Modern

Drummer magazine?” He said, “Yeah, I do.” I said, “Did you see that article about Tiny Kahn?” And I said, “Great article” by I think Burt Korall had written it. And the kid goes, “Yeah I saw it.” I said, “Did you read it?” He said, “No. I didn’t read it.” I said, “Why didn’t you read it?” Are you ready for this? His answer was, “Because I didn’t know who he is.”
There’s a weird loop to that thing.

Yeah. And I just said to this young man, I said, do you realize what you just said? Do you wear the same clothes every day? Do you have the same conversations every day? I mean damn. And the other trick that I would use with them is I put on, I had a deal with my students. They’d give me the stuff they’re listening to, all the current stuff, and I hip them to the stuff that I grew up with when I was their age. So I put on Mahavishnu “Inner Mounting Flame.” Billy Cobham. And this kid goes, “God, who is that?” And I said, “That’s Billy Cobham, and he’s doing that on a four-piece drum set.” “You’ve got to be kidding.”
Yeah. Like in 1972, also.

Something like that, yeah. And I said, “Are you familiar with Billy Cobham?” And of the course the classic answer: “I know his name.” “Okay” I said, “now you’ve got his music, are you excited about this?” “My God” he says, “I can’t believe it, I can’t believe it. I’m going to go check him out.” Okay. So I wait maybe three weeks, three more lessons go by. The student comes in I said, “Okay, I’m ready for it.” He goes, “What’s that?” “Tell me what you found.” And he said, “Found, what do you mean?” “Well Billy Cobham, you said you were going to dig deep into Billy Cobham.” “Oh man, I had an English exam” and blah-blah-blah. And I say now those are the kind of people, I tell them I say, “If that’s how you pursue things that really turn you on” — meaning you don’t pursue them at all — you have no business going into music. Absolutely no business at all. You can do it for fun, become a stockbroker, a doctor, a lawyer, a dentist, anything. But you’re not going to make it if you don’t have — because the people who are your competition, to put it in capitalistic terms, they’re good because they welcome what they don’t know and when then discover what they don’t know they go for it. And if you don’t do that you don’t have a snowball’s chance in hell.
You know you’re very quotable.
I’ve been saying it a long time.

Before we move on, I love little anecdotes about the logistics of things. And I’m borrowing from an interview I saw with you about the wood block and the cymbal. But you said the fact that you were playing percussion or drums along with a stereo system taught you that you had to play with dynamics or you couldn’t hear the music.
Right.
That is just so something.

Yeah, and all the drummers my age — DeJohnette came to school a number of years and I was always preaching to my students, I’m saying, “I hate to clue you in on this but you’re spending thousands of dollars to do what I did at home for nothing.” And so I’m telling — I’d say, “Play along with anything.” “Well there’s drums on there.” “Well good, that’ll keep you honest, you know? It doesn’t get in the way. All it does is show up what you need to work on.” So DeJohnette comes to school. And one of the students goes, “Mr. DeJohnette, did you practice with records when you were a kid?” All right. And DeJohnette says, “Yeah, of course I did. I’d set my drum set up in front of my parents’ hi-fi system,” he said, “my mother’d have to chase me out of the room. I would have stayed there all day and not even gone to school” he said, “I just loved to do that, I’d play all day.” And he turned and started to walk back into the stage area and he whipped around and he said, “And I’ll tell you something, I still play with records.” Yeah.
Excellent.
Yeah. So, and this is — I mean it’s just — that’s another reason why kids go to university is because they get to hear people like that tell them like the way it is you know.
There was a mention here that you played early on with Arnett Cobb?
Oh yeah.
What was that like — not only musically but socially and generationally. How did he speak to you about what he wanted?

Oh he didn’t. I was known as “Little Eddie” because all the guys that I played with when I was coming up — Arnett was — I knew what he wanted because I did my homework and I wasn’t going to try to do my Roy Haynes imitation behind Arnett Cobb. Straight ahead, straight ahead. He was very kind, a man who endured unbelievable pain because of that horrible accident he had. How he stayed on the stage on those crutches or sitting on the stool all night, never went to the men’s room, because it was so difficult for him to get around. But that never came out in his playing or in his personality. Very, very sweet. Very supportive. There were some other guys I played with who were younger who were more — Arnett could have been my grandfather. And these other guys I played with — Jimmy Ford, the great alto player; Don Wilkerson, another great tenor player; and some really incredible Hispanic jazz musicians in Houston who were all old enough to be my dad. My father would take me to the gig and sit there and listen and they would — when the candyman came in the guys would go to the back room with the candyman and say, “Eddie, why don’t you go out and sit with your father for a while.” So they protected me from the seedier elements.
The candyman meaning —
Drug pusher. Yeah.
Yeah.

And these men that I played with were gentlemen, they were very supportive in a much different way than Arnett. I was told Jimmy would whip around and, “What in the hell are you doing back there? Building a house?” Or, “You’re playing so goddamn loud I can’t hear myself. So yeah, that’s where I learned, really. Because thank God those men cared enough, they could have just said, “Get out of here, kid.” But they helped me. They taught me how to play.
Were you sitting in, like there was a regular drummer there?
Yeah.
And they’d make some room for you?

Well what happened was the drummer who had the gig at this particular club that had Sunday afternoon sessions, was a fellow named Dave Berry, who unfortunately has left us, a very sweet man. Hell of a drummer. And it was Dave’s gig and he’d come over to my house a couple of times just to show me some things and then he’d have dinner, and we had a nice relationship. He came over on a break and said, “Eddie, do you want to sit in?” And man I was hoping the floor would open up and I could jump in the hole. Man I said, “No, no.” And my father leaned over and he said, “If you don’t get up and play those drums you’re never going to see your drums again.” So there was no room there for any negotiation. So I got up and I played, and it was really strange because I was so damn nervous I could hardly hold on to the sticks. But after playing the head of the tune and starting to get into the solos, all of a sudden I felt like I was at home playing with records only I didn’t know what was going to come out. But I knew how to play with a bass player because I’d been playing with Paul Chambers and Ray Brown and people like that on record.
You had the cream in your band there.

Yeah. So I got up to leave after the first tune and Jimmy Ford turned around and said, “Hey baby, no man, you sounds fine man, play another tune.” So I played another tune, I played the whole set. And then Dave came over after the gig and he said, “Eddie, the guys really like the way you play, I’m moving to Reno, Nevada in two weeks, would you like to take this gig?”
Oh man.

Yeah. So at the ripe old age of 15 I was playing with the “White Bird.” That’s what they called Jimmy Ford. Those recordings he made with Red Rodney at the Royal Roost, oh my God I’m going, I’m pinching myself.
Yeah you had the classic dream that most of us had at that age and it came true for you.
Yeah. Yeah. And once I got in the network then I started playing — I became a night person, it’s a wonder I made it through school because I was playing a lot of sessions

with a lot of good drummers: Malcolm Pinson; a great drummer named Carl Lott who’s still alive, a great drummer; Richie Lockwood, I don’t know what happened to Richie. But man, and there were at least four or five full time jazz clubs in Houston back then.
Did you get a reputation in your high school like you’re a cool cat, man?
No.
No?

No. Not really. I led a double life. I went to a very good parochial high school, St. Thomas High School. And my father sent me there because he had gone to a parochial high school in Tulsa when he was a kid. He said later with the public schools if you go to St. Thomas you’re really going to get an education, and I did. It was harder than university in some ways. So they had no music program really. They did but it was in its early stages and it really wasn’t happening. So what I was mainly involved in were my sessions and then I played in an incredible youth orchestra. That’s where I got the timpani thing happening, led by a man named Harry Lantz, one of the greatest educators ever, ever, ever, ever. L-A-N-T-Z. Harry Lantz. And this orchestra was so good that Leopold Stokowski, who at the time was conducting the Houston Symphony, would come over and just rehearse us for the fun of it. I mean it was that good. It was an incredible youth orchestra. Sir Malcolm Sargent, when he was in town, came over. So — and so that was a really — that experience, playing under Harry Lantz in that youth orchestra was just as important from the standpoint of discipline and focus, concentration, responsibility, as were those jazz gigs I was playing. So I had it good on both ends. It was just a remarkable situation when I go back and think about it. But like a lot of things, you don’t fully appreciate it ‘til you’re old enough to understand it.

Right. You had said that you learned to play with bass players on that gig, also with records. Can you put into words what that means? Because I was a little surprised along the way here talking to some bass players and drummers that there are times when people are mismatched, that they don’t feel time in the same way. Has that been your experience?

Yeah. I’ve learned a lot. I know when things are right because — I can’t tell you why. It’s a physical sensation and I know when it’s wrong too. So what I did is first of all I realized that my time is not God’s answer to time. And that if I had to be anything, or the only way that I could say that my time is the time is if I’m the leader of the band, obviously. But if I’m a sideman I have to be adaptable and I think that’s one of the joys of playing music with a lot of people is the process of adapting. One has to be a chameleon in a way. And I enjoy that. And I’ve played with bass players and the first tune I go oh God, this guy really plays behind the beat. So what I do is I go with that bass player and lock up at the slower tempo. Now there’s a problem. If when I go down to

where he is, he continues to slow down. That’s a problem. Just like a bass player who plays on top, and when you join him he wants to take off. All right? So I would — like I say I knew when it was hooked up and I knew when it wasn’t hooked up. And I learned to when it wasn’t hooked up sometimes to say on a break to the bassist, “Hey man, how does it feel to you?” And the bassist might say, “Yeah I hate to tell you this but it feels like you’re behind.” And I’ll say, “Well that’s funny because I thought you were ahead.” And we have a good laugh and we re-tune, re-tune. There’s been only one bass player that I have absolutely — I tried everything in my book to hook up with this gentleman and received a call from him the next morning in which he in no uncertain terms told me that I was the worst drummer he’d ever played with.
Wow.

So you realize everybody’s got their own scene, their own perception. And it’s not something I worry about. And when I put on recordings I listen to like Miles’ classic quintet or the quintet with Tony Williams and Ron Carter and those folks, the tempo goes up, the tempo goes down, but it goes up and finds a new niche and stays there. And it goes down and finds a niche and stays there. So — so what? It’s swinging. And that is the beauty of adaptability.

I saw Louis Hayes in New York with this group. And I could not believe that by the time this song was going to be done that it hadn’t sped up by 20 beats per minute or something. Because he was so aggressive and — I don’t know if I even said he’s on top of the beat, I just felt like —
He’s definitely on top of the beat.
On top of the beat.

Oh yeah. He and Sam Jones man together, they were great, because they both felt that. You know along the same lines, when Ray Brown was here a number of years ago we went out to eat some barbeque and I said, “I’m going to ask you a really stupid question.” He says, “I’m used to it.” I said, “Okay.” I said, “Who’s the most comfortable drummer you’ve played with?” And I mean this man played with everybody. And without blinking an eye he said, “Buddy Rich.” I said, “Buddy!” And I said, “Why?” He says, “Because we both felt the time in the same place.” Cutting edge of the beat. Way on top. And he said, “I’ll tell you something else,” he said, “Buddy Rich is the only musical genius I ever met.” Yeah. Put that in your pipe and smoke it. And I said, “Why?” And he said, “Because I never met anybody who had the type of ears that he had.” And he told an anecdote where I think it was Dizzy who brought Ray up and told Ray to come to New York. And Dizzy took Ray down to a theater where the Dorsey band was playing between shows. And Buddy was playing drums. And Ray said this was the first time he’d heard Buddy live. And he sat there and they were rehearsing a singer’s act. And the

singer was all pissed off because Buddy wasn’t reading the chart and evidently wasn’t playing things that the guy wanted, was supposed to play. So Dorsey turned to the singer and said, “Don’t worry, it’ll be fine tonight.” So Ray came back for the show that night and he said that Buddy played things that even he didn’t hear could be played. And you know Rich’s aural (A-U-R) memory is the equivalent of a photographic memory. He could hear something once — Joe LaBarbera, who used to rehearse new charts for the band — Buddy would sit out front and Joe’d play it down once and Buddy’d say, “Let me try that.” And Joe said Holy Christ you know, he did it, amazing. Amazing. Yeah. And then following on the idea about Ray and Buddy feeling the time in the same place, Ed Thigpen told me that Ray Brown just gave him hell when Ed first joined the trio with Oscar because Ed couldn’t play on top of the beat enough for Ray. So he said we’d have a location gig somewhere and before Ray would go out and play golf in the afternoon we’d get up in the morning and go down to the club and rehearse, just playing time, until I could put it up there where he wanted it. So yeah, it’s fascinating. It’s really fascinating.

Along those same lines, I’m going to read a quote here from a bass player named Neal Caine, who is a fairly young man, I think he’s from New Orleans, a marvelous player who played here. And he was addressing the issue — I think I asked him about bass solos.
Mm-hmm

And he says, “When you think about the fact that we spend our whole careers making everyone else sound good on their solos and then we get our solo and the drummer goes to the hi-hat and the piano player just sits there. It’s infuriating to me.”
Yup.

And I wanted to ask him what he liked but, so if there’s a question here, if you’re on a date, especially where it’s one of those dates like meet the group on the bandstand, hi how are you doing, and it comes time for a bass solo, what’s your inclination to do?

Well if it’s appropriate stylistically — I’ll just put it this way — if it’s a swing gig, Benny Goodman sort of music, Basie kind of music, straight ahead 4/4, more than likely the bass player is going to expect you to go to the hi-hat.
That’s what Neal said.

Yeah. But I learned, Rufus Reid and I have played off and on together for years. It’s got to be close to 40 years now that we’ve known each other. And the first time I played with Rufus — because when you first meet him he’s a pretty intimidating guy. A big guy with a low voice who speaks slowly. Look out. And I went to the hi-hat behind his solo. And he looked at me and man it was like Mount Vesuvius had erupted. He says, “Don’t do that, treat me like a horn player dammit.” And that was it. Back to the ride cymbal, comping, the whole thing only on another dynamic level of course. So and to this day
there are still times when I’ll approach the bass solo like that but the bass player will say, “Hey man, I’d really like it if you’d just go to the hi-hat.” So again —

Has a drummer ever told you to just not play? Because that’s what happens a lot of times, you know the old joke about everybody starts talking during the bass solo, I think it’s partly because everybody else drops out.
Well I don’t drop out unless the bass player asks me to.
Yeah.

No, I might go to brushes just for the dynamic difference, or I just might play sticks softly, but I do, just like Rufus said, treat it like a horn solo. But people, everybody else stops when the drum takes his solo. That’s what kills me.
Okay. Good point.

Yeah. Except, you know and Max Roach tried to change that a bit because the bass player would continue walking the changes of the tune on some of those recordings and Max would play over that, which is like saying hey, you know, I get a bass line too. But the majority of drum solos, I mean that’s a chance for the guys to go to the bar. So when I have my group, my little groups that I put together down here, I’ll tell the rest of the band, “Play behind me the same way you play behind a horn solo.” And I say to the horn player, “You can comp, comp on your horn.” And it’s not the usual way but at my age you don’t want to do things the usual way. And when you’re playing predominantly with young people, which is what I do, I do very little playing with my own age group you know, they’re open for anything. So it’s fun and they — that’s just sort of a side story about how drummers are treated. I’ll tell you one funny story: Mel Lewis, God rest his soul, I went to hear him play with some really good horn players in Connecticut where I was living at the time. And he’s laying time down behind these people, just I mean a dead man could swing it sounded so good. And then it came time to trade fours and eights and Mel did some things man that, you could see the horn players [counts] and their eyes getting big and when they came in it was all staggered. And Mel did this through the whole sequence. It was the last tune of the set, the finish. I go up to say hello to Mel and he’s surrounded by the horn players. They’re all bitching at him, “Mel, what the hell are you playing on your fours and eights. I couldn’t tell the time.” And Mel looked at them and said, “Look man, I sit up there and spend the majority of my time going ding-ding-a- ding-ding-a-ding behind your solos, so when it comes time for my solo I can play whatever in the hell I want to play. Case closed. Yeah, drummers’ rights.
All right. I’m going to be careful how I look at my drummer tonight. You know I was talking to Phil Wilson about you.
Oh wow.
I had a wonderful conversation with him a couple of months ago, and I phoned him before this interview and I said, “Why did you pick Ed for that album you did about the wasp?”
“The Sound of the Wasp.” Yeah.
Yes. And he said, “Well for one thing he’s got a great sense of humor” and etcetera and etcetera, but he said, “I like the way he played the crotch cymbal.”
The crotch cymbal.
A crotch cymbal.
Yeah. You know what that is?
I think — is it the Chinese cymbal?
Exactly.
All right.
Yeah. I had forgotten that he called it the crotch cymbal.
Yes. But he said, you know, you have the touch and he likes the way that particular thing sounds, you can build on it. And he said something about — the pitch was lower so it didn’t get in his way.

Exactly. Yeah. Yeah there’s all sorts of things that, oh I mean you open a real can of worms — that’s why drummers have so many cymbals, unless they’re the leader of the band and can pick you know. But I mean the cymbals that you use for a big band probably you’re not going to use for a small group, although Buddy Rich would kick me for saying that because when you’re in a big band, when you play behind a soloist it immediately becomes a small group. But in the case of say if I’m playing in a guitar trio I have the cymbal sound in my ear that I think will go best with that kind of timbre.
So when I see drummers, if you’re coming from out of town and you book a concert like you have to have a drumset for me, but they come in carrying their cymbal bag.
Right.
And do you suppose they have chosen those cymbals particularly for that gig usually?

I don’t know it’s usually just something that — to have one’s own cymbals when playing strange drums is a very important comforting mechanism, and especially ‘cause it’s — drums you can, yeah, you can get by fixing them pretty easily. But if you’ve got bad cymbals it just doesn’t work.
That’s right. You can’t tune a cymbal, right?
No. Unh uh.
Unless you have that ball peen hammer.

Right. I only know of one drummer who likes playing on cymbals he’s never played on before. He’s a great drummer, a great musician, Joey Baron. Joey welcomes it because he says, “Every time I play on a different kit with different cymbals it forces me to play in a
different way. And man I just like — wow. Yes. Definitely. So you know there’s a positive side to everything.
When you got on the Woody Herman band was there — were you ready for it and did it fulfill your expectations?

Oh and more. Yeah that was, working for Woody was — well working with both Woody and Kenton were both wonderful experiences, diametrically opposed in musical approaches. But I was ready for both of those bands because I did my homework. But Woody’s band, to me, was like a big small group. The writers that he had were so good. Alan Broadbent, Tony Klatka, and Bill Stapleton. Great charts. And Woody’s willingness for the rhythm section to try new things. You know the album that a lot of people talk about is “Giant Steps.” And from a drummer’s standpoint, drummers — well [Jeff] Hamilton said that that album opened up a whole new door for big band drumming. And the reason why was because the rhythm section, it was Wayne Darling bassist and Andy LaVerne pianist, we decided to play like a jazz trio even behind the ensemble and sort of go beyond traditional roles as it were, especially from the drum standpoint. Repetitive four on the bass drum and repetitive hi-hat on two and four, and that kind of thing. And the first time we started doing that, we couldn’t do it on the all the charts, we did, like we played “Four Brothers” we played that style. But if we played “La Fiesta” or “Countdown” or any of the newer charts we’d approach it from a freer perspective. The first time we tried it the trumpets completely folded on the shout chorus of the tune. And the lead trumpet player was ready to kill me. In fact Sid told me that he would kill me if I ever did that again to the band. And Woody, who, he was called “Road Father” for a reason, he was a very wise man. He’d seen about everything. And he came up to me and he said, “I know what you’re trying to do, just do it a little more gradually.” And that’s what we did. We just eased into it. And it worked.

That’s really interesting because on occasion I’ve asked some musicians who played very, I’ll call it experimental music sometimes free jazz. If they sat down and talked about it first, like okay let’s play without bar lines and this kind of thing, and normally they said no, it just happened. But in this case you’re saying the three of you made a conscious decision to play in a different manner.

Yeah. A different style. Yeah. For sure. I’ll tell you, big band drumming is a dream and it’s a shame that opportunities are so scarce now unless you go into the Army or the Air Force and play in a service band. Because I realized that every night, unlike the fifth trumpet player, I could approach a chart differently. I didn’t have to play the same fills all the time, unless it was something that was crucial to the arrangement. But I could leave things out. I could play more. I could play less. And so every night it was great because it really forced me, and the whole rhythm section for that matter, to really use our

imaginations. Because if you don’t use your imagination that’s when you get bored. And I mean you lived for those, you had 22 hours off and two hours on, you know? And you’d ride that damn stinking bus for hours just in anticipation of getting on the bandstand and going after it. And every night was a new experience. Sometimes good, sometimes not so good. But at any rate it was there. And that’s what — Woody loved that. There were times when I would deliberately leave out a big fill that I usually played and the band wouldn’t come in right after that because they were so dependent upon the fill. And Woody would just laugh his ass off because he knew that’s how you keep the band in line, keep them listening.
Yeah there was an early jazz writer, Whitney Balliett, I think he said, “Jazz is the sound of surprise.”
Yeah, exactly, yeah. So Woody was fine with that sort of thing.
So is it harder to play slow music than fast music, or vice versa?
Either one is hard.
Okay.

Not really. I learned that too, when with Kenton’s band you had to push. Because Kenton’s band was like dragging a dead water buffalo through the mud. I mean it was so brass heavy you know. And I don’t say that in a disparaging way. It had its own way of swinging, it was just sort of lugubrious swing.
Lugubrious swing. There’s another quote from Ed Soph.
But now Stan was a great leader. And the band was a real challenge in many ways, which would be another six hours. But — now I’ve lost my train of thought when I was coming back to Woody’s band.
Well we were talking about swing and Stan.

Yeah. Woody’s band I mean — playing slowly, that’s it yeah — one of the first nights we played “Early Autumn” which obviously featured the saxes. And the lead tenor player, a great musician who is still with us, Frank Tiberi. Frank Tiberi would lay back so far on the beat it’d almost put you back a year. I mean he just [scats]. So one of these early nights I decided to go with the saxophones instead of keeping the pulse, I tried to phrase with them. And Woody goes, “No, no, no! Keep it up, keep it up!” All right? The only way, and I realized the only way that one gets the impression of them of the saxes laying back is if the rhythm section stays put, like the same idea with Basie. Those horns are laying back but Sonny Payne is back there on top of it like a son-of-a-gun.
And Freddie Green.

And Freddie Green. Yeah. So you learn that contrast is an important part of the music, that everybody doesn’t necessarily have to play the same time. So learning that was good. I’ll never forget that. We’d have contests too to see how fast we could play “Caldonia.”
And Don Switzer, who was the bass trombonist on the band, had a stopwatch and he’d time the choruses. Oh man.

I have a brief quote from an interview with Sam Noto. And he was with the Kenton band. And he said they were in New York and Count Basie’s band was at Birdland so they all went down there. And Stan went as well. So the next day they’re on the bus and Al Porcino says, “Stan, I saw you at Birdland last night, how did you like Count Basie’s band?” And Stan says, “Oh it was great but all they do is swing.”
That’s good.
But you know Kenton’s arrangements were — many of them were not really meant to swing like Woody Herman or Basie.
Oh of course. Of course, yeah, definitely. Yeah.

Let me ask you, go back to your teaching for a minute. If you can think back to the start of your career, the early years, an advice that you might have given a senior — or a junior or a senior drummer who, you know like a music major, how might it be different from the advice you would give near the end of your teaching career?

Oh jeez. I can’t answer that. I don’t know. I’ll tell you why I can’t answer it. It’s because everybody’s different. And my philosophy became, when I first started out and how I related to a student is I was dead set on making this person the greatest drummer in the world, and which I realized later on was just a huge ego trip on my part, so that I could say I created that drummer. And I realized that not everybody is meant to be the greatest drummer in the world — whatever that means — but I realized that my job was to enable a person to achieve whatever potential they can. And because with potential comes enjoyment. And that’s why I play music, it’s because I enjoy it and that’s why anybody plays music or listens to music, because they enjoy it. So I realized by putting undue pressure on someone who really didn’t have the ability or basic skills to ever play what I thought would be well, I was depriving them and turning the whole experience into a very negative thing. So as the longer you teach the more you pare away all the B.S., your personal B.S. And the first step was to realize, was to pinpoint a person’s musical weaknesses and try to make them, instead of being limitations, turning them into advantages, without any consideration of how good this person is going to play. That’s out of your hands. That’s up to the individual how they apply themselves. But my basic job was to give everybody the same tools. I have a good friend who’s a teacher and also primarily a great player. And I saw him a number of years ago and I said, “Are you still teaching?” And he said, “No, no I’ve given up on that.” I said, “What do you mean you’ve given up on that?” He says, “Oh I show the kids all my stuff, they move to New York and do their own thing.” And that’s the kind of teacher — I would be horrified to be that kind of teacher because my whole point in teaching, and maybe the greatest credit to

my teaching is none of my students play like me. I mean that’s the greatest compliment ever that a teacher can be given. And they’re all distinct personalities. Everybody — take Ari Hoenig and Keith Carlock — ooh, night and day. You know? Rich Redman, the country drummer? Night and day. But they’ve all got the same skills and they all applied them in their own way. Not my way, their way. It’s just like you teach somebody language. They learn how to use it their way. That’s the same thing you do with music, with drumming in this case. So that’s the evolution of my teaching is sort of — well it didn’t sort of, it took that tack.
What a path you’ve had. Would you have ever, under the guise of making a living, taught students or addressed students about programming drum machines?
No.
Okay.

I don’t have that skill. And I was, quite frankly, too enamored with the drums themselves to even take the time to learn the technology. Because I had things I needed to work on just from my own musical standpoint. And so yeah, the changes in the past 40, 50 years have been remarkable. And in a lot of ways I think the way I learned, primarily through mentorship, I hope isn’t lost with what’s coming down the pike with all the artificial intelligence technologies. And it’s — I’m sure there will always be mentors, I certainly hope so. And if perhaps a whole new type of art form will evolve out of whatever we’re moving into. I mean it’s such a period of transition with what is on the horizon. If it’s not climate change it’s technology. You know, it’s just incredible what these young people have in front of them. That was the other thing too is to make these people aware not in a negative way but in a realistic way, you know learn about the world for Christ’s sake because you’re going to be living in it. And be aware of what’s going on. Develop your critical thinking skills, you know it’s not just about being able to play a quarter note equals 400. You’ve got to have a healthy environment in which to make your music.
Maria Schneider said much the same. She said you have to live life in order to put it into your music.

Yeah, exactly. So yeah, self-realization is, well you can help a student with that. And what I found as a teacher is that the more you can relate to your own development, the problems that you had when you were their age or younger. I mean that helped me remarkably is to think about now what I would have done if I were his age and confronted with this. And drawing on my own experience, that’s why those days of playing with Jimmy Ford and Arnett was so valuable is because it gave me so much, I mean oh God, it’s just such an education, such an education. Every day, like wow, that’s what he meant.
That’s what he meant. Do you remember what you made on your first paying gig?
Oh, probably fifty bucks.
That’s a lot.

Which was a lot of money back then, yeah. Yeah man, I paid my way through St. Thomas, paid my own tuition I’m proud to say, and I graduated from college without any student debt. Now that’s the other thing, these poor kids, man, that was — it wasn’t that, I’d say man I’d go to Dallas, I’d work seven nights a week when I was in school and making on the average $60 to $75 a night. My rent was $60 a month. I’d work one gig my rent was paid. And so yeah, there’s something to be said for those good old days. Because I’d drive to Dallas to play a gig, a jazz gig, a fun gig, and make damn near the same money I made when I was in school only maybe I make $75 instead of $60. Plus tips of course.
Ah yes. Did you ever play “Wipe Out” for tips?

Yeah, yeah. And my students now, the ones who are successful, very few are successful just playing drums. There’s so many other avenues that are necessary to — especially if they have families. Some of them become website builders. A lot of them have very lucrative teaching practices. I was talking to one of my former students who was a very inventive, creative individual but who supports his music by teaching. And he charges something like $125 an hour. And I say, “My God, do kids have that much money?” And he says, “Oh I’m not teaching kids.” I said, “Well who are you teaching?” “I’m teaching doctors, lawyers, stockbrokers, guys who go home and have drum dreams.”
Yes, they probably have the most expensive drum sets too.
Exactly. Yeah. Oh man, yeah. So I’m thinking right on, go for it, you know?
Oh this has been a wonderful conversation and as I said you’ve said some marvelous things about teaching and being a professional, and I really appreciate the time you spent with me.
Oh my pleasure. I’m honored to be in such great company.
Yeah we have a nice list of drummers.
Oh man, musicians period, it’s just crazy. I had no idea the scope of it. It’s great.
Well thank you, Ed. I hope we cross paths sometime in the future —
Well if you’re ever down in the Dallas/Ft. Worth area let me know.
Okay.
Yeah. Stay well.
Thank you. Over and out.
Okay. Bye-bye.

segments.title: Interview opening and Hamilton notes
segments.summary: Copyright notice, biographical note and Monk Rowe's Zoom interview details.

segments.title: North Texas State and switching to an English major
segments.summary: Soph recalls North Texas in 1963-68 before jazz degrees, why he left music for English, and his timpani hopes.

segments.title: Supportive parents and his father's record collection
segments.summary: His father, a jazz fan and ragtime player in Tulsa, backed him; his first gig was on woodblock with his father.

segments.title: The hubcap cymbal
segments.summary: As a six-year-old he hammered a neighbor's Packard hubcap into a cymbal and got in trouble; he dreamed of a drumset.

segments.title: Nursery school rhythm sticks, home records and church music
segments.summary: His love of rhythm began in a nursery school marching band; at home his father played records and took him to Tulsa jazz gigs and a church.

segments.title: Whether rhythm is innate
segments.summary: Asked about natural ability, he says everyone has potential and describes the range among his 32 North Texas students each semester.

segments.title: Teaching jazz by ear: singing a Parker tune on the snare
segments.summary: He explains his aural teaching method, having students vocalize 'Billie's Bounce' and then translate it to drums.

segments.title: Getting students to listen to the past: Baby Dodds
segments.summary: Soph says students resist older recordings; he recalls wearing out his father's LPs and his first hero Baby Dodds.

segments.title: The student who did not know Tiny Kahn, and Billy Cobham
segments.summary: Anecdotes of students lacking curiosity, including one who never explored Billy Cobham, and Soph's warning about commitment.

segments.title: Playing along with records; DeJohnette's visit
segments.summary: Practicing with a stereo taught dynamics, and Jack DeJohnette tells students he still plays with records.

segments.title: Playing with Arnett Cobb and Jimmy Ford in Houston
segments.summary: As 'Little Eddie' he played with Arnett Cobb and older Houston musicians who protected and taught him.

segments.title: Sitting in at fifteen and taking Dave Berry's gig
segments.summary: His father makes him sit in on a Sunday session, Jimmy Ford approves, and Dave Berry hands him the gig.

segments.title: Houston sessions, St. Thomas High and Harry Lantz's youth orchestra
segments.summary: Houston drummers and clubs, his parochial high school and the youth orchestra under Harry Lantz.

segments.title: Feeling time with different bass players
segments.summary: He explains adapting to bassists who play behind or on top of the beat, and Miles's quintet shifting tempo.

segments.title: Louis Hayes, Ray Brown on Buddy Rich, and Ed Thigpen
segments.summary: Stories of drummers on top of the beat, Ray Brown calling Buddy Rich the most comfortable drummer, and Thigpen's time rehearsals with Brown.

segments.title: Drummers behind bass solos; Rufus Reid
segments.summary: Responding to Neal Caine's quote, Soph says to treat bass solos like horn solos, a lesson from Rufus Reid.

segments.title: Drum solos and Mel Lewis on trading fours
segments.summary: He treats drum solos like horn solos, cites Max Roach, and tells Mel Lewis's 'drummers' rights' story.

segments.title: Phil Wilson and the crotch cymbal on The Sound of the Wasp
segments.summary: Rowe relays why Phil Wilson chose Soph for his album: humor and the Chinese cymbal sound.

segments.title: Choosing cymbals; Joey Baron
segments.summary: Cymbals for big band versus small group, drummers bringing their own cymbals, and Joey Baron's different attitude.

segments.title: Joining Woody Herman and the Giant Steps rhythm section
segments.summary: Soph describes the Herman band's writers, the trio-style approach on the Giant Steps album, and Sid and Woody's reactions.

segments.title: Big band drumming and keeping the band listening
segments.summary: He loves the freedom of big band drumming, life on the bus, and leaving out fills to keep the band alert.

segments.title: Kenton's lugubrious swing
segments.summary: Slow versus fast, and Kenton's brass-heavy band as dragging a water buffalo; Stan was a great leader.

segments.title: Frank Tiberi, Basie's contrast and Caldonia contests
segments.summary: Woody tells him to keep the pulse behind the saxes' laid-back phrasing, like Sonny Payne and Freddie Green with Basie.

segments.title: Kenton on Basie: all they do is swing
segments.summary: Rowe reads Sam Noto's anecdote about Stan Kenton hearing Basie, and they agree Kenton's charts were not meant to swing.

segments.title: Evolution of his teaching philosophy
segments.summary: He moved from trying to make the greatest drummer to enabling each student's potential; none of his students play like him.

segments.title: Drum machines, technology and learning about life
segments.summary: He never learned drum programming, hopes mentorship survives AI, and advises students to learn about the world.

segments.title: First paying gig and paying his way through school
segments.summary: His first gig paid about fifty dollars, and he paid his own tuition with Dallas gigs at $60-75 a night.

segments.title: How his students make a living
segments.summary: Few students live on playing alone; many teach, including one charging $125 an hour to adult hobbyists.

segments.title: Thanks and goodbyes
segments.summary: Rowe thanks Soph, who says he is honored; they say goodbye.
